title: DeDNS-over-DeVPN
tagline: DDoV: anonymous browsing via attested, no-log relays - paid per-session on Arc via x402.
description:
DDoV (DeDNS-over-DeVPN) is a marketplace for anonymous internet access with enforceable, revocable permissions. A user pays for a time-boxed session at a chosen bandwidth tier (Lite/Standard/Turbo), and their device opens an encrypted tunnel to an authorized relay operator. That operator's tunnel-termination, DNS-resolution, and outbound-proxy logic runs inside a Chainlink CRE confidential handler, so the operator's own machine cannot read or log the user's traffic - attested and independently verifiable, not just promised.

Which relays are currently authorized lives in an ENSv2 registry (hierarchical subnames like bob.dvod.eth) that separates the operational key (updates endpoint/capabilities) from the payout address (where earnings go), so a compromised operator key can't redirect funds. A permissionless watchdog contract - not a human admin - automatically revokes any relay whose attestation report stops matching its published, audited build hash, and the client fails over to a healthy relay within seconds.

When you pay for a VPN with a your card, the payment itself ties your name to the service - you're exposing exactly the identity a VPN is supposed to protect. Paying in crypto avoids that: no card, no name, no linkage back to you, which is why DDoV settles exclusively through Arc/x402 rather than any card rail. Since payment is x402-gated and settles in USDC on Arc, as a single batched per-session purchase - never a per-packet or per-DNS-query transaction, so the latency budget for live browsing stays intact.

The one-line pitch: browse without your ISP, your relay operator, or the sites you visit ever being able to link "who" to "what" — provably, not on our word. It's a full VPN-shaped privacy layer, not DNS-only, and the README states plainly which pieces (ENSv2, Chainlink CRE, Arc/x402, automatic vs. manual revocation) are genuinely live versus honestly labeled as simulated at demo time.
how_its_made:
DDoV is a pnpm + Turborepo TypeScript monorepo, built spec-first: the architecture, phase plan, and design system are laid out up front and drive implementation phase by phase, with small feature-branch commits merged into dev and tagged phase-completions merged into main -never a single end-of-day dump.

The shared type layer (packages/session-spec) uses Zod to define the session, tier, and ENSv2 capability-record schemas, plus an explicit session state-machine transition table (BROWSING → QUOTED → PAID → TOKEN_ISSUED → TUNNEL_OPEN → ACTIVE, with RELAY_REVOKED/RELAY_UNREACHABLE both routing through an automatic FAILOVER_SELECT) so every transition is validated in code, not just diagrammed.

Four partner technologies each do one job, deliberately non-overlapping: ENSv2 hierarchical subnames + permissioned resolvers register relay operators and separate their operational key from their payout address, so a compromised operator key can never redirect earnings; Chainlink CRE runs the tunnel/DNS/proxy logic inside a confidential, attested handler so the operator's own machine can't read traffic; Arc settles USDC; x402 gates session purchase/renewal only - never per-packet - to keep DNS/browsing latency real.

The design system enforces its own discipline in code: an --accent token is reserved by convention to exactly three UI moments (countdown, tier highlight, failover/revocation), documented alongside the token values themselves rather than left to hope.
auto_summary: A monorepo for buying time-limited privacy relay sessions, managing relay identity in ENSv2, and refreshing attestation data via Chainlink CRE.
